beats.got: Finally a number. 11 to 6 to 3 is checkable before and after. It's still not money. 45 minutes is also a lot of my day.

beats.got: I generate a briefing and have it scored. It's a doing step, but on a generic briefing, not my material.

beats.trigger: Now step away. Come back to a tactic tightened by a judge you did not move.
beats.got: Thirty minutes of waiting while it runs. Asking about 'model-training analogies' while waiting is not for me.

beats.got: There's a hash check proving the checker wasn't altered. That is audit-trail thinking, the first thing I'd trust.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: Each round improved the instructions from the last round's errors, and no one was present. Nice, but what did it cost in tokens?

beats.got: I'd own the standard rather than check each output. That's how I run finance already, so it's not new.

beats.trigger: Ask the agent to set up the loop around a different judge:
beats.got: I could do the same with another checker. 'Convergence was the floor' means nothing to me.

beats.trigger: The judge had stopped finding things. That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: A zero error count doesn't mean it's good. Right, a clean audit isn't a good business.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: When the metric goes flat, the metric may be the limit. This is the KPI trap I've seen in three programmes.

beats.trigger: Where it passed something you would have sent back, the judge and you do not agree as often as the number suggests.
beats.got: Score a handful by hand and compare with the machine. That's a sample test I can specify to my controller, and it's the most useful thing here.

beats.trigger: The rest is yours to name.
beats.got: Models will fabricate less, so the judge must check something else. The slide ends with a vague 'yours to name'.

beats.trigger: Files are the handles. Connectors bring material in. Agents read and write. Judges hold a line. Loops make the next session sharper.
beats.got: A recap of eight modules in slogans. The snake game is irrelevant to me.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?
beats.got: A concrete question: what must be true before an agent sends an internal mail in my name. It's a risk-first framing, and that works on me.

beats.trigger: An ungrounded mail is a trust problem. A grounded but vague or tone-deaf mail is a usefulness problem.
beats.got: Two kinds of failure: untrue and useless. Repeats the earlier slide.

beats.trigger: the generator makes more than you need, the judge discards most of it, and the tactic file keeps what survived.
beats.got: It generates a lot, discards most, and keeps the best. That means paying for output that gets thrown away.

beats.trigger: The answer may be draft only, review first, send to yourself first, or automatic when the groundedness judge passes and the goal-nudger scores high. Some categories never go without a human.
beats.got: A ladder from draft-only to automatic, with some categories always needing a person. That is an approval matrix I can take to IT and the works council.

beats.trigger: Two judges now sit on disk: one keeps the work grounded, one steers it toward your standard.
beats.got: I make a second checker for mail. Mail isn't my pain, month-end variance is.

beats.trigger: Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops.
beats.got: Success makes you stop watching, which is how control failures happen. They named a risk before I raised it.

beats.trigger: If the answer is a month, put one in your calendar.
beats.got: Put a date in the calendar to read one output end to end. Simple and doable.

beats.trigger: Your role in the loop is to design the conditions under which the system earns more autonomy, one loop at a time.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a summary slide with a figure and a slogan.

beats.trigger: If it sounds too kind, ask: *"Which rule did you claim to remove but keep under another name? Quote both lines."*
beats.got: Challenge the agent's summary and make it quote lines. That's how I'd treat a consultant's deck.

take_homes: A checker only means something if it can't be changed by whoever is being checked, and you can prove it didn't change with a hash.
A flat or clean score can mean the metric is blind. Score a sample by hand against the machine's verdicts before trusting it.
Decide in advance what the agent may do alone and what always needs a person: draft only, review first, automatic.

monday.move: Ask my controller to run the month-end variance commentary through an agent once, and have her score ten claims by hand against the source figures.
monday.who: Controller, plus me reading the result
monday.when: Month-end close, not before IT approves the tool for finance data
monday.stop_condition: If hand-checking finds figures that don't trace to the ledger, or it costs more than the hours saved
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and I still have no cost per user per month.

misconception.why: The module never gave a cost, a payback or a licence comparison. Everything was about building and running loops, which I read as more things to buy and run. The 'design the loop and own the yardstick' idea touched it, but only in passing.

one_line: The fixed-judge and check-the-checker parts are sound and I could defend them, but there's no cost or payback figure anywhere, and half the module is slogans.
